Hi Samir — quick technical note based on typical Redwood runtime behavior and options for POC sizing:

1) Scale-up times (typical ranges):
- Cold allocation of a new GPU worker (no warm image): ~3–6 minutes (depends on cloud image boot and model load time)
- Warm pool -> hot worker (model already resident): ~15–45 seconds to accept traffic (depends on model kv-cache warming and warm pool size)
- Fast-path (pre-warmed & warmed kv-cache): <10s to route traffic if capacity reserved

2) Warm pool sizing guidance:
- For Helios baseline/avg qps 120 and burst to 600, recommend a warm pool sized to handle ~40–60% of expected peak burst (e.g., warm pool = capacity for 240–360 concurrent sessions) so initial burst is covered while autoscale ramps
- Warm pools reduce p95 significantly — our measurements show p95 start-to-first-byte reductions from ~700ms (cold) to ~120–180ms (warm) for sample conversational models

3) Queueing & graceful degradation:
- Default behavior: short (configurable) queue with head-of-line priority; requests beyond queue size are rejected with a clear 429 and fallback option can be triggered
- We can configure a fallback routing policy: route to a smaller (quantized) model variant or reduce streaming token rate to maintain start-of-first-byte SLOs

4) POC recommendations:
- Provision a 24–48hr warm pool sized at ~30–40% of peak to evaluate real burst coverage
- Use live traffic trace (anonymized) to run a dry-run and simulated burst test — this gives accurate cost & latency curves
- We’ll provide a sample autoscale policy and a cost delta estimate for warm pool vs 100% on-demand (attached CSV with estimates)

I attached a short CSV with ballpark numbers for warm pool sizes and expected p95/TBFB; we’ll refine after we see your trace. Happy to jump on a 30m deep-dive next week.

Cheers,
